docs.title: My Documentation
docs.text: This site is a record of my learning journey in the Modeling & Fabrication course, where design and making converge to spark innovative solutions. It is built with Markdown, which means you can easily edit and update content directly in GitHub. All changes are tracked with Version Control using Git, so every version of your documentation is safely stored.

docs.title: About Me
docs.text:
I am Niyomugenga Grace, pursuing a Master of Science in IoT Embedded Computing Systems (ECS) at UR-ACEIoT. I am driven by a passion for digital fabrication, modeling, and the creative fusion of technology with problem-solving.

My work reflects my growth as an IoT engineer and embedded systems developer, with digital fabrication as a cornerstone for hardware prototyping and firmware integration. From PCB design to crafting physical enclosures, I explore how embedded systems evolve from abstract concepts into tangible products. Each step I document highlights the process of bridging software logic with hardware realities, shaping me into a firmware developer who thrives at the intersection of design, engineering, and fabrication.

docs.title: Digital Fabrication Revolution
docs.text: Digital fabrication links digital design and physical production through computer-controlled tools such as CNC machines, laser cutters, and 3D printers. It evolved from manual craft and industrial manufacturing to enable rapid prototyping, precision, iteration, and hybrid workflows—transforming fabrication into an accessible process for innovation, education, and localized production.

docs.title: Course Structure
docs.text:
This 9-day intensive course covers the complete digital fabrication workflow, from foundational concepts to advanced multi-process integration:

  1. Foundations – Modeling principles and fabrication ecosystems
  2. Digital Modeling – CAD workflows and Design for Manufacturing (DFM)
  3. PCB Design – Circuit design and milling techniques
  4. Materials – Properties, selection, and fabrication methods
  5. Subtractive Methods – CNC and laser cutting
  6. Additive Methods – 3D printing technologies
  7. CNC Routing – Advanced sheet fabrication
  8. Molding & Casting – Replication processes
  9. Integration – Final projects and documentation

docs.title: My Journey
docs.text:
Born and raised in Rwanda, I discovered an early fascination with electronics and communication technologies. I began cultivating hands-on expertise through professional training in fiber-optic installation and troubleshooting, which gave me a practical foundation in connectivity systems.

I earned my Bachelor’s degree in Electronics and Telecommunication Engineering from the University of Rwanda, College of Science and Technology (School of Engineering). Building on this academic and technical base, I am now advancing my skills in embedded systems and IoT—focusing on the integration of electronics, communication, and smart connected devices.

My journey is driven by a commitment to transforming theoretical knowledge into practical, real-world applications that improve everyday life and empower communities.

docs.title: 1. Activity of Day 1: Introduction to Modeling and Fabrication Design
Summary
docs.text: Day 1 introduces the foundational concepts bridging design intent and physical reality. I explored the design-to-fabrication continuum and contemporary digital fabrication paradigms that shape modern making practices, then established the CO3 nameplate project scope.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Understand the relationship between digital modeling and physical fabrication
  • Learn the design-to-fabrication continuum: Design → Model → Prototype → Fabricate → Evaluate
  • Identify key digital fabrication paradigms and their applications
  • Recognize how fabrication methods shape design decisions from conception
  • Set up professional documentation workflow using MkDocs

docs.title: Why Modeling & Fabrication Matter
docs.text:
Contemporary design practice has fundamentally shifted. Design today is computational, material-driven, and production-aware. Fabrication is no longer merely an end step—it actively shapes design decisions from the earliest conceptual stages.

Key Applications: - Architecture: Parametric facades, robotically fabricated structures - Product Design: Rapid prototyping, mass customization, user-centered iteration - Engineering: Simulation-driven design, additive manufacturing - Research: Physical computing, material experimentation, speculative design

docs.title: The Design-to-Fabrication Continuum
docs.text:
Design follows an iterative cycle, not a linear path:

Design → Model → Prototype → Fabricate → Evaluate → [Repeat]

Critical Insight: This process is iterative, not linear. Feedback occurs at every stage, and failure serves as a powerful learning tool.

Phase Description Design Conceptualize and define intent, goals, and constraints Model Create digital representations encoding design logic Prototype Build physical tests to validate assumptions Fabricate Produce final artifacts using appropriate methods Evaluate Assess outcomes and gather learnings for next cycle

docs.title: Digital Fabrication Paradigms
docs.text: Contemporary fabrication methods fall into four primary categories:

docs.title: Subtractive Fabrication
docs.text:
Process: Removing material from solid stock through cutting, milling, or drilling

Technologies: CNC milling, laser cutting, waterjet cutting, lathe turning

Advantages: - High precision and accuracy - Excellent surface finish - Wide material compatibility

Constraints: - Material waste - Limited to 2.5D without multi-axis machines - Tool access limitations

Materials: Wood, metals, plastics, foam, composites

docs.title: Additive Fabrication
docs.text:
Process: Building objects layer-by-layer through material deposition

Technologies: FDM/FFF, SLA/DLP, SLS, binder jetting, material jetting

Advantages: - Complex geometries without additional cost - Minimal material waste - Design freedom and internal structures possible

Constraints: - Visible layer lines - Support structures required - Material limitations - Post-processing often needed

Materials: PLA, ABS, PETG, nylon, resins, metals (specialized), ceramics

docs.title: Formative Fabrication
docs.text:
Process: Shaping material through force, heat, or pressure using molds

Technologies: Casting, vacuum forming, injection molding, bending, stamping, thermoforming

Advantages: - Material efficiency - High-volume production capability - Organic, flowing forms

Constraints: - Requires tooling/molds (upfront cost) - Draft angles required - Undercut limitations

Materials: Plastics, metals, concrete, composites, textiles, elastomers

docs.title: Hybrid Fabrication
docs.text:
Process: Combining multiple fabrication paradigms sequentially or simultaneously

Examples: - 3D printed molds for casting - Additive + subtractive machining - Laser-cut assembled components with 3D printed connectors

Advantages: - Optimizes strengths of each method - Increased geometric complexity - Material diversity in single object

Constraints: - Workflow complexity - Multiple machines/skills required - Alignment challenges

Key Insight: Fabrication method is a design choice, not an afterthought. The selected paradigm influences geometry, materiality, cost, sustainability, and aesthetic expression. Expert designers think through fabrication from the earliest conceptual stages.

docs.title: 2. Activity: Building Documentation Website with MkDocs
Overview
docs.text:
I set up a documentation website using MkDocs with Material theme to record and showcase all course activities, design processes, and fabrication experiments. This documentation serves as both a learning tool and a professional portfolio.

Documentation as Design Practice: Documentation is not an afterthought—it is part of the design process itself. Through documenting work, you develop clarity of thought, communicate complex ideas, and contribute to the collective knowledge of the design community.

docs.title: Step 1: Install Prerequisites
docs.text:
# Install Python 3.8 or later
# Download from https://www.python.org/

# Install MkDocs and Material theme
pip install mkdocs-material

Requirements: - Python version 3.8 or later - pip (Python package manager)

docs.title: Step 2: Create a New MkDocs Project
docs.text:
# Create new documentation project
mkdocs new fabrication-docs

# Move into project directory
cd fabrication-docs

This creates the following structure: 

fabrication-docs/
├── mkdocs.yml
├── docs/
│   └── index.md
└── README.md

docs.title: Step 3: Enable the Material Theme
docs.text:
Edit mkdocs.yml to enable Material theme and configure basic settings:

site_name: CO3 Nameplate Documentation
site_description: Foundations of Modeling & Fabrication
site_author: Your Name

theme:
  name: material
  palette:
    primary: blue
    accent: light-blue

docs.title: Step 4: Write Documentation Content
docs.text:
All documentation pages are written in Markdown format. Place files in the docs/ directory:

docs/
├── index.md
├── Daily-Activity/
│   ├── day_1.md
│   ├── day_2.md
│   └── ...
├── images/
│   └── day_1/
│       └── ...
└── stylesheets/
    └── extra.css

docs.title: Step 5: Configure Navigation
docs.text:
Define site navigation in mkdocs.yml to organize pages hierarchically:

nav:
  - Home: index.md
  - Daily Activities:
    - Day 1: Daily-Activity/day_1.md
    - Day 2: Daily-Activity/day_2.md
    - Day 3: Daily-Activity/day_3.md

docs.title: Step 6: Preview the Website Locally
docs.text:
Run the development server to preview changes in real time:

mkdocs serve

Open your browser to http://127.0.0.1:8000 to view your site. Changes auto-reload as you edit files.

docs.title: Step 7: Enable Material Features (Optional)
docs.text:
Add advanced Material theme features to mkdocs.yml:

theme:
  features:
    - navigation.tabs
    - navigation.sections
    - toc.integrate
    - search.suggest
    - content.code.copy

docs.title: Step 8: Add Recommended Markdown Extensions
docs.text:
Enable markdown extensions for richer documentation:

markdown_extensions:
  - admonition
  - tables
  - attr_list
  - md_in_html
  - pymdownx.details
  - pymdownx.superfences
  - pymdownx.highlight
  - toc:
      permalink: true

docs.title: Step 9: Build the Static Website
docs.text:
Generate static HTML files for deployment:

mkdocs build

This creates a site/ directory containing all HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files ready for hosting.

docs.title: Step 10: Deploy to GitHub Pages
docs.text:
Deploy your documentation website to GitHub Pages:

mkdocs gh-deploy

Prerequisites for Deployment: - Project must be in a Git repository - Must have GitHub account and repository - Requires write access to repository settings

Alternative Deployment Options: - Netlify - Vercel - Local server - Traditional web hosting

docs.title: Digital Modeling for Fabrication
docs.text: I created a parametric 3D CAD model of the CO3 nameplate in FreeCAD, establishing the precise geometry for all subsequent fabrication steps.

docs.title: Activity 1: Parametric Base & Sketch Development
docs.text: I created the base geometry using a parametric ellipse (150mm × 90mm) with 10mm extrusion. I then developed detailed sketches for the letter geometry, iterating through multiple design approaches to achieve optimal proportions.

docs.title: Activity 2: Final Design & Verification
docs.text: I finalized the design, verifying all critical dimensions: oval 150×90mm, base 10mm thick, letter depth 4mm, and corner radii 2mm for tool clearance. The design uses a 4mm pocket operation for letter carving.

docs.title: Activity 3: Export & Format Conversion
docs.text: I exported the model in multiple formats for downstream fabrication: STEP (for CNC milling), STL (for 3D printing prototype), and DXF (for laser-cut template validation). Each format was verified to maintain dimensional accuracy and fabrication constraints.

docs.title: Technical Documentation & Quality Control Planning
docs.text: I created comprehensive technical documentation for the CO3 nameplate project, including detailed engineering drawings, dimensional specifications, and quality control inspection plans to ensure fabrication accuracy throughout the manufacturing process.

docs.title: Activity 1: Preliminary Design Verification
docs.text: I verified all design specifications and constraints established on Day 2. This stage involved checking CAD model dimensions, confirming tool clearances (2mm radii for 4mm end mill), and preparing technical documentation packages for downstream fabrication activities.

docs.title: Activity 2: Technical Drawing Development
docs.text: I generated professional technical drawings including orthographic projections (top, front, side views), section views, and detailed dimensioning following industry engineering standards. All critical dimensions specified with tolerance callouts: ±0.1mm for letter depth, ±0.5mm for overall dimensions, and appropriate surface finish notes.

docs.title: Activity 3: Quality Control Planning & Inspection Strategy
docs.text: I developed a comprehensive quality control (QC) inspection checklist covering three phases: pre-fabrication verification (material and tooling checks), in-process monitoring (dimensional verification during machining), and post-fabrication final inspection (surface quality, tolerances, assembly fit). Measurement methods specified for each feature using calibrated instruments.

docs.title: Activity 4: Bill of Materials & Cost Analysis
docs.text:
I compiled a complete bill of materials (BOM) including all components required for the project: raw materials (walnut hardwood blank), cutting tools (6mm and 4mm end mills, laser-cutting consumables), finishing supplies (progression sandpaper 120-400 grit, stain, polyurethane), and miscellaneous fasteners. Total estimated project cost calculated including material, tooling, and finishing materials.

Note: 3D Printing Not Performed

The 3D printing prototype validation step was not completed due to a broken micro drill bit. This required reassessment of prototype validation strategy. The prototype validation was instead addressed through laser-cut template verification on Day 5.

docs.title: Materials & Fabrication Methods
docs.text: I evaluated four candidate materials (plywood, hardwood, aluminum, acrylic) against design criteria and selected walnut hardwood for its optimal balance of aesthetics, machinability, and durability for the final CO3 nameplate.

docs.title: Activity 1: Material Options Evaluation
docs.text: I tested and compared: Plywood (cheap, easy to machine), Hardwood (premium appearance, harder to machine), Aluminum (industrial look, requires coolant), Acrylic (modern, risk of melting). Created a weighted decision matrix considering appearance (30%), machinability (25%), durability (20%), cost (15%), learning value (10%).

docs.title: Activity 2: Material Selection Decision
docs.text: Walnut hardwood scored highest (4.1/5): rich chocolate color, machines cleanly at 18,000 RPM with 800mm/min feed, takes stain beautifully, and creates a portfolio-quality final piece. Selected walnut as final material over plywood (inferior appearance) and aluminum (too difficult for learning).

docs.title: Activity 3: Fabrication Parameters Planning
docs.text: Determined CNC milling parameters for walnut: spindle speed 18,000-20,000 RPM, feed rate 800mm/min for roughing and 600mm/min for finishing, 1mm stepdown for roughing and 0.25mm for finishing. Ordered 160×100×12mm walnut blank (~).

docs.title: 5. Activity of Day 5: Digital Fabrication I - Laser Cutting & Template Validation
Introduction
docs.text:
Digital fabrication technologies allow designers to convert digital designs into physical objects using computer-controlled machines. In this session, I used laser cutting to fabricate a 1:1 template of the CO3 nameplate outline.

Laser cutting enables precise manufacturing of parts from various materials such as cardboard, acrylic, plastic, and wood. This session emphasized how digital designs created using CAD software can be directly used to fabricate real-world components and prototypes.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Laser cutting uses a focused laser beam to cut or engrave materials with high precision. It is widely used for 2D fabrication and rapid prototyping. Laser cutting works best with vector designs, which can be created using cutting machine software like Lightburn or Inkscape.

The CO3 project uses laser cutting as a validation step: creating a 1:1 cardboard template to verify proportions and dimensions before committing to expensive CNC milling in walnut.

docs.title: Preparing Designs for Fabrication
docs.text:
Before sending a design to a fabrication machine, several preparation steps are necessary:

  • File Preparation: Ensure correct design dimensions and scale. Export from CAD in vector format (DXF, SVG).
  • Machine Settings: Configure cutting speed, laser power, tool diameter, and cutting depth based on material type and thickness.
  • Vector Setup: Create closed paths with proper stroke styles (red = cut, blue = engrave) for laser machine interpretation.

Important parameters are cutting speed, laser power, and material thickness. These parameters depend on the material type being cut.

docs.title: CO3 Laser Cutting Process
docs.text:
I exported a 2D DXF file from FreeCAD containing the oval outline (150mm × 90mm) without depth data. I imported the design into Lightburn laser software, set the red stroke for cutting, and positioned it at the laser bed center.

Machine Parameters: - Material: 3mm corrugated cardboard - Laser Power: 60% - Cutting Speed: 25mm/s - Air Assist: ON

The laser cut through the cardboard cleanly in approximately 90 seconds. I then measured the result with digital calipers: 149.8mm × 89.9mm, which represents a deviation of only -0.2mm—well within acceptable kerf tolerance for laser cutting.

docs.title: Design Validation & Mockup Testing
docs.text: Holding the cardboard template at eye level, the proportions looked perfect. I sketched the C, O, 3 letter positions on the template with pencil to verify 5mm letter spacing. No crowding or aesthetic issues were evident. The design validation confirmed that the project is ready to proceed to the 3D printing prototype stage.

docs.title: Key Learning Points
docs.text:
From this laser cutting session, I learned:

  • How digital designs are converted into machine instructions
  • How material properties influence fabrication processes
  • Basic safety procedures when operating laser cutting equipment
  • The importance of rapid prototyping in design validation

Safety

Ensure proper ventilation during laser cutting and never leave machines unattended while operating. Wear appropriate eye protection and ensure the work area is clear of obstacles.

docs.title: Dimensional Verification Results
docs.text:
Dimension Target Measured Deviation Status Width (mm) 150.0 149.8 -0.2 ✓ Pass Height (mm) 90.0 89.9 -0.1 ✓ Pass

All measurements are within acceptable tolerance ranges for laser cutting (±0.5mm typical). The design is validated and ready for subsequent fabrication stages.

docs.title: Digital Fabrication II: Additive Manufacturing
docs.text: This session focused on additive manufacturing using an Ultimaker 3D printer. The goal was to prepare a digital model for printing, slice it in Cura, run the print, and inspect the final PLA prototype.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Additive manufacturing builds parts layer by layer from digital files. For Day 6, the process started with an STL model exported from CAD, then moved through slicing, printer preparation, and print quality inspection.

docs.title: Preparing the Model for Printing
docs.text:
The CAD model was exported as an STL file and imported into Ultimaker Cura. The chosen print settings were:

  • Layer height: 0.2 mm
  • Infill: 20%
  • Nozzle temperature: 205°C
  • Bed temperature: 60°C
  • Adhesion type: brim

After slicing, Cura generated the G-code for the Ultimaker printer.

docs.title: Printing and Monitoring
docs.text: The build plate was leveled, PLA filament was loaded, and the print started. The first layers adhered well, and the print progressed steadily with no visible failures.

docs.title: Prototype Evaluation
docs.text: After printing, the part was removed from the bed and the brim was trimmed. The printed object showed the expected FDM layer texture and the overall shape matched the original design.

docs.title: Final Result
docs.text: The completed prototype was evaluated for surface quality and dimensional accuracy. This prototype validated the 3D printing workflow before moving to the next fabrication stage.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• How to prepare and slice a 3D model for a PLA print
  • How to configure Ultimaker Cura print settings
  • How to monitor a print job from start to finish
  • How to inspect a printed prototype for quality and validation

docs.title: Digital Fabrication III: CNC Router Milling & Cutting
docs.text: In Day 7, I worked with a 3-axis CNC router to machine the final CO3 nameplate from walnut hardwood. The process covered CAM toolpath preparation, machine setup, cutting execution, and final inspection.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: CNC milling removes material from a workpiece using toolpaths generated from a digital design. For this activity, the machine followed a program that controlled the router on multiple axes to cut the nameplate accurately.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: CNC operations require strict safety practices. I kept my hands away from moving tools, monitored the machine continuously, and confirmed that the workpiece was securely clamped before starting the cut.

docs.title: CAM Toolpath Preparation
docs.text: The design was imported into CAM software, and the cutting strategy was defined. Typical steps included roughing to remove bulk material, finishing to refine the letter surfaces, and profiling to cut the final part outline.

docs.title: CNC Execution
docs.text: The walnut blank was secured on the bed and the router was zeroed to the material surface. The machining sequence started with the roughing pass, followed by a finishing pass, and finished with the profile cut to free the nameplate.

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text: During the toolpath generation stage, a problem occurred when the CNC software attempted to create the cutting path. The toolpath was damaged, making the instructions unusable by the CNC machine. This issue was identified during preparation and required revising the machining setup before proceeding.

docs.title: Inspection and Results
docs.text: After machining, the part was removed, the tabs were trimmed, and the nameplate was inspected. The final piece showed accurate dimensions and clean letter details, demonstrating the CNC workflow from design to finished part.

docs.title: Finishing & Surface Enhancement: CO3 Nameplate Completion
docs.text: I transformed the raw CNC-milled walnut into a polished, museum-quality finished nameplate through progressive sanding, dark walnut staining, and multi-coat polyurethane sealing.

docs.title: Activity 1: Progressive Sanding (120 → 220 → 400 grit)
docs.text: Sanded with 120-grit to remove CNC tool marks (15 min). Wiped dust, sanded with 220-grit to remove 120-grit scratches (15 min). Final sanding with 400-grit using light pressure created silky-smooth surface (10 min). Result: Glass-smooth walnut, ready for stain. Touch-tested: fingernail no longer catches on any surface marks.

docs.title: Activity 2: Dark Walnut Staining
docs.text: Applied Minwax Dark Walnut oil stain using foam brush (3 min application). Let penetrate for 8 minutes, wiped off excess with cotton rag. Walnut transformed from pale tan to rich chocolate brown; grain patterns now dramatically visible. Let cure 4-6 hours until not tacky.

docs.title: Activity 3: Protective Polyurethane Coating (3 coats)
docs.text: Applied water-based satin polyurethane coat 1 (2 hrs dry), light-sanded with 320-grit, applied coat 2 (2 hrs dry), sanded, applied coat 3. Final cure: 24 hours. Result: Satin sheen, silky-smooth surface, protected for years. CO3 nameplate now looks like a high-end furniture piece with professional finish.

docs.title: Final Presentation & Course Reflection
docs.text: I compiled complete project documentation and reflected on the 9-day journey from CO3 nameplate concept to finished walnut product, documenting lessons learned and techniques mastered across digital fabrication methods.

docs.title: Activity 1: Complete Project Documentation Assembly
docs.text: Assembled final documentation package: CAD files (FreeCAD, STEP, STL, DXF), CAM toolpaths (G-code), technical drawings (PDF), bill of materials, QC checklist, process photos (120+), and time-lapse video. Total project cost: .42 (walnut \, finishing \, prototyping .42). Active work: ~15 hours; passive time (printing, drying, curing): ~33 hours.

docs.title: Activity 2: Before/After Transformation Documentation
docs.text: Photographed CO3 evolution: Day 1 sketch → Day 2 CAD model → Day 5 cardboard template → Day 6 PLA prototype → Day 7 raw CNC walnut → Day 8 finished walnut. Tested lighting angles (overhead, 45° side, backlighting) to showcase letter depth and grain patterns. Finished piece looks professional and exhibition-ready.

docs.title: Activity 3: Lessons Learned & Skill Mastery
docs.text:
Key Takeaways: (1) Iterate in cheap materials first (cardboard .50, PLA ) before expensive final (walnut ), (2) Parametric CAD enables rapid refinement, (3) DFM thinking prevents fabrication disasters, (4) CNC precision (±0.1mm) combined with hand finishing creates museum-quality results, (5) Documentation is part of design—reproducibility matters.

Skills Acquired: Parametric solid modeling (FreeCAD), CAM toolpath generation (Fusion 360), laser cutting (CO₂ cutter), 3D printing (FDM), CNC milling (3-axis router), finishing craftsmanship (sanding, staining, sealing), technical documentation standards.
